action_criteria.expected_evidence: Evans index 0.32 with temporal horns enlarged out of proportion to the hippocampi (MTA 1); callosal angle 96 degrees, not acute; DESH absent; Fazekas grade 2 white matter change; patent aqueduct with flow void; no obstructing lesion
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for ventricular size, iNPH supportive features and an obstructing cause
action_criteria.rationale: Fourteen months of gait, urinary and cognitive decline with an outside report of enlarged ventricles need an MRI that measures the ventricles, looks for supportive features and excludes obstruction before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, TSH, vitamin B12 and folate; RPR and HIV non-reactive
action_criteria.label: Targeted labs for reversible contributors
action_criteria.rationale: A thyroid, B12 and metabolic screen is reasonable in her cognitive slowing but does not decide the iNPH question.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 28 s with walker, 10-metre walk 22 s in 30 steps, 180-degree turn in 6 steps, start hesitation and en-bloc turning not explained by the knees
action_criteria.label: Baseline timed gait assessment before the tap
action_criteria.rationale: With a walker, near-falls and a knee replacement, an objective baseline is needed both to measure the tap response and to separate the magnetic gait from the knee.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 21/30 with attention, working-memory, fluency and free-recall deficits, recall improving with cues
action_criteria.label: Bedside cognitive screen
action_criteria.rationale: Her daughter reports slowing and word-finding difficulty, so a MoCA documents the cognitive profile and the tap baseline.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 14 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; 40 mL removed; TUG 28 to 24 s at 2 hours and 21.5 s at 24 hours (23%), 10-metre walk 22 to 17 s, MoCA 21 to 22
action_criteria.label: Lumbar tap test with opening pressure and CSF removal
action_criteria.rationale: With a callosal angle that is not acute and no DESH, the tap response is the main evidence for probable iNPH and for shunt benefit.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 24 s at 2 hours and 21.5 s at 24 hours (23% faster); 10-metre walk 17 s at 24 hours (23% faster); MoCA 22/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the same timed measures with the same walker at 2 and 24 hours gives a comparable number for her response.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented
Do not attribute the gait disorder to the knee osteoarthritis or the left knee replacement
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 23% in TUG at 24 hours, the supportive MRI (Evans index 0.32 with temporal horn enlargement) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: She has no episodes suggesting seizures, so an EEG cannot separate iNPH from its mimics.
Her near-falls are mechanical, without syncope or palpitations, so an ECG does not inform the gait work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
An MRI is available and measures the temporal horns, callosal angle and aqueduct better than CT.
The near-falls are not syncopal, so rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Normal-pressure CSF with a normal cell count in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas grade 2 white matter change can add to gait and executive slowing, but ventricles enlarged out of proportion to it, enlarged temporal horns and a 23% TUG improvement after the tap make iNPH the main cause.
Mild ankle tone increase without rest tremor, cogwheeling or upper-limb bradykinesia, and a gait that improved after CSF removal, argue against parkinsonism.
Attention and fluency deficits with cued recall, hippocampi of MTA 1 and a gait-first course do not suggest Alzheimer's disease as the main cause.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: The callosal angle of 96 degrees is not acute, but ventricles out of proportion to the sulci, temporal horns out of proportion to the hippocampi and a tap response argue against atrophy ex vacuo.
There is no history of head trauma, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis or intracranial surgery.

key_clinical_evidence: Insidious gait disturbance over 14 months from age 70 with urge incontinence and cognitive slowing, and no antecedent trauma, haemorrhage or meningitis, meets the clinical criteria for probable iNPH [Relkin_2005]

MRI shows Evans index 0.32 with temporal horns enlarged out of proportion to the hippocampi and a patent aqueduct; the callosal angle (96 degrees) is not acute and DESH is absent, so the temporal horns are the supportive imaging feature [Relkin_2005] [Nakajima_2021]

Opening pressure 14 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL was removed, TUG improved 23% at 24 hours (28 to 21.5 s) and the 10-metre walk 23%, above the commonly used 10% TUG criterion [Nakajima_2021]
Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with a PPV of 73% to 100%; a positive tap supports shunting, while a negative one would not have excluded it [Marmarou_2005]
Fazekas grade 2 white matter change makes a vascular contribution likely but does not preclude a shunt response [Tisell_2011]
Her depression is in remission on sertraline; the attention and fluency deficits with cued recall fit the iNPH profile and are not explained by mood
The left knee replacement and knee osteoarthritis do not produce start hesitation, en-bloc turning or a response to CSF removal

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Knee osteoarthritis and the left knee replacement can cause pain and an antalgic gait, but not the broad-based, short-stepped gait with start hesitation and en-bloc turning that improved after CSF removal.
red_herrings.data_point: Osteoarthritis bilateral knees (total knee replacement left 2 years ago)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait difficulty is attributed to knee osteoarthritis and the knee replacement

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

patient.chief_complaint: Gait instability, 'slowness' of thought, and urinary urgency for 14 months

family_history: No family history of dementia or neurological disease
past_medical_history: Osteoarthritis bilateral knees (total knee replacement left 2 years ago)

patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old right-handed retired nurse with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and history of left knee replacement was admitted from the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of 14 months of progressive gait difficulty, urinary urgency and cognitive slowing. The patient, a former nurse who is knowledgeable about her own health, first noticed gait changes approximately 14 months ago — she describes her feet as feeling 'like they are stuck to the floor' and she began using a walker after two near-falls in the home. She notes that her gait instability is disproportionate to the bilateral knee pain — she has had worsening bilateral knee osteoarthritis but her orthopedic surgeon told her that her gait pattern is 'not just the arthritis.' Over approximately the same period she has developed urinary urgency that occasionally results in urge incontinence before reaching the bathroom. She wears pads 'just in case.' Her daughter has noted she is more 'vague' and 'slow to respond' in conversations over the past 8 months — she repeats herself more and takes longer to find words than previously. A brain MRI obtained as an outpatient at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles and white matter disease; the images are not available.

neurological_exam.additional: No resting tremor. No cogwheel rigidity. Pull test: one step backward but recovers without falling (mildly impaired postural reflexes).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly awkward bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, 3mm, reactive. EOMs full. Facial sensation intact. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, short-stepped gait. Reduced foot clearance. Takes 4-5 steps to initiate. Turns en bloc requiring 5-6 steps. Unable to perform tandem gait. Uses walker.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented, with slowed responses. Speech mildly slowed but fluent. Word-finding mildly impaired. No apraxia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild bilateral lower extremity stiffness — increased tone at ankles. Upper extremity tone normal. Strength 5/5 throughout. No tremor.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ biceps, brachioradialis. 2+ patellar bilaterally. Achilles 1+. Plantar flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration mildly reduced at ankles. Joint position sense intact at toes.
